prompt:
TASK: READ ONE INSTRUMENT ENTRY AND ANSWER THREE QUESTIONS

Below is one entry from the specification of a web measurement instrument. The instrument checks
public websites of U.S. federal statistical agencies and reports, per agency, whether each check
passed or failed. The entry states the check's question, the behavior a ready publisher is
expected to show (with verbatim quotes from the sources it cites), the test the instrument runs,
and what a pass and a fail claim.

Terms the project defines once for every entry (they are not undefined): SI client (SI system): a system that finds, reads and uses data on its own, such as an answer engine, an agent or a retrieval pipeline; the project's term for what is elsewhere called an AI system; data page: an agency's own web page for one data product, the page the harness measures (also 'product page' in rule code); harness: this project's scanner: an identified, robots-compliant HTTP client that fetches the pages and records what it met; cycle of record: the scan whose results the published grid is built from (here scan_2026-10-07_composite_d); recorded location: an address for an agency's API, terms, changelog or inventory that the harness was given, read from the agency's own pages or seeded from a named source; error / not measured: the harness could not observe: an access denial, its own robots compliance, an absence it could not confirm, or a server or network error; never a fail; leg: one check as the harness runs it, named by its indicator code (A1, D4); each leg has one rule, and the codes in a test field name other legs whose fetches this one reuses; rule / branch: the versioned code that turns observations into a verdict; a branch is one way the rule can reach a verdict, with its own reason text; Observation: one recorded fetch (request, response, parsed content) that a rule judges; surface: the page a verdict is about: a data page, or for site-level checks the agency's home host; body: the agency, as the harness's records name it; complete search: an absence is reported as a fail only when every candidate location was observed and every named source searched; otherwise the verdict is error (DN-012); seed source: a named place a recorded location came from: the agency's own developer page, catalog.data.gov, api.data.gov, this repository's citations, or a model's knowledge, each recorded per location; params.*: a named parameter in the harness's configuration file (assessment/harness/scan/params.yaml); its value is stated where it matters

Answer from the entry alone. For question 1, the QUOTED SOURCE PASSAGES are the only evidence of
what the sources say; do not use what you know of them from elsewhere.

1. Does the EXPECTED BEHAVIOR come from the cited sources and not from the writer? Answer "yes"
   if every requirement the expected-behavior text attributes to a source is supported by a
   quoted passage, and any part no source defines is said plainly to be undefined or the
   project's own. Answer "no" if it states as a source's requirement something the passages do
   not contain; name it.
2. Could a reader who knows the agency misread a FAIL on this check as a claim the test did not
   make? Answer "yes" if the CLAIMS leave such a misreading open (name it), "no" if they close it.
3. Is any term in the entry undefined for a technically literate reader new to this project?
   Answer "yes" and list the terms, or "no".

Return ONLY a JSON object, with no prose before or after it and no code fence:
{"q1": {"answer": "yes" or "no", "why": "..."}, "q2": {"answer": "yes" or "no", "why": "..."}, "q3": {"answer": "yes" or "no", "terms": ["..."], "why": "..."}}

ENTRY
CHECK: A5 (RULE-A5-v2)

QUESTION:
Is the data page listed in the host's sitemap? Search engines and answer engines discover pages by following links and reading sitemaps; on a large site, a page a sitemap omits can go undiscovered, and an SI client cannot cite a page its retrieval layer never found.
Established by: omb-m-23-22-digital-first-public-experience (§III.4: agencies should employ best practices to improve crawling or indexing of web content, including using sitemaps); sitemaps-protocol (Sitemaps are a way for webmasters to inform search engines about pages on their sites that are available for crawling)

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR:
Federal agencies should employ best practices to improve crawling or indexing, including sitemaps (M-23-22 §III.4, quoted). The sitemaps protocol defines the file: its location bounds the URLs it may list, it may be declared in robots.txt, and it is expected to list URLs from a single host only (quoted). Google defines what a sitemap is for: it "tells search engines which pages and files you think are important in your site" (quoted); a site of about 500 pages or fewer that is comprehensively linked might not need one, and on large sites it is harder to make sure every page is linked (quoted). The check takes an agency's data page to be among the pages its owner thinks important; that premise is the framework's, not a source's.
Cited sources: omb-m-23-22-digital-first-public-experience (§III.4); sitemaps-protocol (Sitemap file location; Specifying the Sitemap location in your robots.txt file); https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/sitemaps/overview (Do I need a sitemap?)

QUOTED SOURCE PASSAGES (verbatim):
- [omb-m-23-22-digital-first-public-experience] "Agencies should employ best practices to improve crawling or indexing of web content, including using sitemaps, robots.txt files"
- [sitemaps-protocol] "The location of a Sitemap file determines the set of URLs that can be included in that Sitemap."
- [https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/sitemaps/overview] "You might not need a sitemap if"
- [https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/sitemaps/overview] "in most cases, your site will benefit from having a sitemap"
- [sitemaps-protocol] "You can specify the location of the Sitemap using a robots.txt file."
- [sitemaps-protocol] "a Sitemap is expected to have URLs from a single host only"
- [https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/sitemaps/overview] "You might not need a sitemap if: Your site is "small". By small, we mean about 500 pages or fewer on your site."
- [https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/sitemaps/overview] "Your site is comprehensively linked internally."
- [https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/sitemaps/overview] "Your site is large. Generally, on large sites it's more difficult to make sure that every page is linked by at least one other page on the site."
- [https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/sitemaps/overview] "A sitemap tells search engines which pages and files you think are important in your site"

TEST:
Client: the harness's identified, robots-compliant client
Request: GET /sitemap.xml, /sitemap_index.xml, the sitemap(s) robots.txt declares (same site only), /llms.txt and /.well-known/ discovery paths; parse sitemaps with ultimate-sitemap-parser
Reads: whether any served sitemap lists the data page's URL
Decision rule:
- pass: `sitemap at {url} lists the product URL`
- fail: `discovery files served ({urls}) but none lists the product URL`
- fail: `no sitemap, llms.txt or well-known discovery file served`
- not_applicable: the host declares a sitemap on another site, which the harness records and does not fetch
Parameters: a URL matches when it equals the data page's URL as the frame records it
Is it the recognized way to measure the behavior: Reading the sitemap and looking for the URL is what a crawler does with it (sitemaps protocol). No published method defines a pass/fail for "the page is listed"; the harness's rule (listed or not) is the direct reading.

BRANCHES (each verdict branch of the rule; the behavior it rewards or penalizes; its source):
- pass_listed_in_sitemap (pass): a sitemap served on the host lists the data page Source: omb-m-23-22-digital-first-public-experience (§III.4); sitemaps-protocol (protocol).
- fail_served_but_not_listed (fail): the host serves a sitemap or llms.txt that does not list the data page Source: omb-m-23-22-digital-first-public-experience (§III.4); https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/sitemaps/overview (Do I need a sitemap?).
- fail_no_discovery_file (fail): the host serves no sitemap at the probed locations Source: omb-m-23-22-digital-first-public-experience (§III.4).

CLAIMS:
A pass claims: A sitemap served on the agency's host lists this data page's address, exactly as the harness records it.
A fail claims: The host's sitemaps were read and none lists this data page's address in exactly the form the harness records (a trailing slash, redirect target or query-string variant does not match), or the only discovery file served is an llms.txt (which by its proposal summarises a site rather than listing every page), or no sitemap is served at the standard locations. The reason names which. It is not a claim that the page is absent from the sitemap in every form, nor that search engines cannot find the page: well-linked pages are found without a sitemap.
Neither claims: Nothing about whether the page is indexed by any engine, or about sitemaps on other hosts.

CONFOUNDS:
- the sitemap lists the page under a different URL form (trailing slash, redirect target, query string). Distinguished: no: a fail.
- the only discovery file served is llms.txt, which by its proposal summarises a site rather than listing every page. Distinguished: no: the served-but-not-listed branch does not separate llms.txt from a sitemap in its verdict, only in its reason's URLs.
- the sitemap is declared on another site. Distinguished: yes: not_applicable.
response_text: {"q1": {"answer": "yes", "why": "Each attributed requirement maps to a quoted passage: the M-23-22 'best practices ... including using sitemaps' sentence; the protocol's location-bounds-URLs, robots.txt declaration, and single-host passages; Google's 'which pages and files you think are important', the 'about 500 pages or fewer' and 'comprehensively linked' conditions, and the large-site linking difficulty. The one premise no source supplies (that a data page is among the pages the owner thinks important) is explicitly labelled the framework's own. The only looseness is that the writer joins Google's separate 'small' and 'comprehensively linked' bullets with 'that is', which the passages neither confirm nor contradict as conjunctive; it does not add a requirement."}, "q2": {"answer": "no", "why": "The fail claim enumerates the three ways a fail arises (exact-form URL not listed, only llms.txt served, no sitemap at the standard probed locations), says the reason text names which, and expressly disclaims the likely misreadings: that the page is absent in every URL form, that search engines cannot find it, that it is unindexed, or anything about sitemaps on other hosts. The test's parameter line and the confounds list repeat the exact-match limitation, so a reader who knows the page is listed with a trailing slash or as a redirect target is told the fail is only about the recorded form."}, "q3": {"answer": "yes", "terms": ["frame (in 'as the frame records it')", "/.well-known/ discovery paths (which paths are probed is unstated)", "llms.txt / 'its proposal' (described in passing, no source cited)", "ultimate-sitemap-parser (named library, not described)"], "why": "'Frame' is not among the project-wide definitions (harness, surface, data page, recorded location are) and the entry does not say what it is or how its recorded URL differs from the data page's URL.
